measurement.happened:
This week in France was dominated by several major themes unfolding simultaneously.

PROTESTS AND SOCIAL UNREST: The single biggest story was the wave of anti-government protests that began earlier and escalated sharply this week. On November 9 there were clashes in Paris after new protests broke out. By November 10, Macron publicly condemned violent incidents while students vowed to keep up pressure. On November 14, more than 100,000 people rallied across France in what were described as new Yellow Vest protests, and Reuters ran a feature on how the anti-government protests spiraled out of control. Student protesters specifically demanded better learning conditions. The government responded on November 9 by bringing forward a hike in the minimum wage to calm the crowds. TV5Monde ran a video titled 'France, la somme des menaces hybrides' and a separate video questioning whether Russia amplified the domestic contestation. The protesters chanted against inflation and police. This was a multi-front social uprising touching students, workers, and the broader public.

IRAN FRIDGE CYBERATTACK: A bizarre and highly publicized incident dominated foreign news. France accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of carrying out an 'unprecedented' cyberattack on supermarket refrigerators across Europe. France summoned Iran's ambassador and warned of a response. Iran denied any involvement. US Treasury Secretary Bessent tied the fridge attacks to a Chinese AI model, adding a third-country dimension. CNBC reported France was weighing sanctions. The French official narrative was that the Shahid Kaveh unit was responsible. This became a major diplomatic friction point and raised broader questions about hybrid threats to French infrastructure.

PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION 2027 - CANDIDATES EMERGING: The political race for 2027 heated up. Judo star Teddy Riner officially announced his candidacy, pledging to bring people together, and Macron welcomed his entry. Riner then pushed back against being labeled a 'Macronist,' calling the president's congratulations a 'poisoned kiss.' Eric Zemmour announced he would stand, saying he wants to 'conserve une France française.' Mélenchon was reported as eyeing a 2027 runoff against Le Pen. A poll showed ECB's Lagarde would rival centrists in the race. Sarkozy warned France faces a financial crisis, possibly before the presidential election. The Made in France salon became a stage where Le Pen, Tondelier, and other figures made their positions heard.

FOOTBALL AND RUGBY: In football, France suffered a 3-1 loss to Italy in the Nations League, giving new coach Zidane his first defeat. Mbappé was ruled out due to injury, Thuram was also out with a hamstring problem, and Upamecano left the squad for personal reasons. In rugby, France delivered a stunning 21-19 victory over world champions South Africa in the Nations Championship, with Antoine Dupont at fly-half after only one training session. The win was described as a 'cornerstone' for the World Cup campaign. Italy's Kane set an England appearance record in a separate match.

ECONOMY AND MARKETS: The economic picture darkened. Moody's cut France's 2026 growth forecast to 0.2 percent. AFP reported the economy was 'headed for a wall' as GDP shrank. The central bank said France would dodge a year-end recession, but the margin was thin. French bonds came under pressure, with the FT noting France and Belgium fell foul of the Eurozone bond market's new divide. ECB's Lane said French bond trouble must be fixed in Paris. The government's minimum wage hike was partly an economic stimulus. Coty announced a restructuring of its French business. IG Group closed offices in France, Spain, and Italy. China booked French and Argentine wheat as global prices slumped. The government allocated 725 million euros to relaunch French agriculture and inaugurated the country's largest green hydrogen plant in the Aude.

DIPLOMACY AND INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS: G7 foreign ministers met in Paris to discuss Iran, Ukraine, and AI, with the US seeking Europe's greater say in Ukraine peace talks. France asked the European Commission to look into Algeria trade issues, and exports to Algeria continued to collapse amid diplomatic tension. France criticized Israel's 'demagogic' move to ban hard-left leader Mélenchon from entering the country. France and Germany agreed that Spain's de Cos should succeed Lagarde at the ECB. France pressured Germany over nuclear risks of long-range missiles. A project linking Cyprus to the EU grid was set to restart with French diplomatic help. France's foreign minister said they favored adding pressure on Yemen's Houthis. France launched a G7+ ports alliance targeting global narcotics routes. The French-speaking nations held a summit in Cambodia as an African conflict threatened a rift. France's Macron visited Angkor, highlighting France's custodial role in heritage.

AL FAYED PROBE AND CRIME: Police searched the Paris Ritz and Villa Windsor in the ongoing probe of the late Mohamed Al Fayed, with arrests made. A De Beers jewelry store in Paris was robbed in broad daylight, with luxury goods worth hundreds of thousands taken. A shooting suspect in France was reported to have targeted Muslims and Africans, a case that reignited debates about colonial history and racial violence. A body was found on a French beach after an attempted Channel crossing.

CULTURE, SPORTS, AND OTHER: Actor Gérard Depardieu withdrew his appeal against a sexual assault conviction. Wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre died aged 104. The Sotheby's sale of a Pissarro painting was annulled by a Paris court. A two-year-aged French Comté cheese won World Cheese of the Year. A wildfire tore through the Fontainebleau forest near Paris. France banned eel fishing. A warning was issued over thousands of substandard condoms. Two French guards collapsed as the Slovak president arrived in Paris for a meeting with Macron. The Macrons filed a new lawsuit against US podcaster Joe Rogan. Russia banned two French lawmakers and two journalists in a tit-for-tat move. The EU was set to approve more sanctions on Russia on Monday. A note listing four left-wing figures was found at the home of a suspect in Trappes. The French army ministry announced plans to set up a center for defense-related AI. France and India discussed cooperation in space and critical technologies. Disney and Skydance were eyeing TV rights bids for French football Ligue 1. France's 2030 Winter Olympics saw leadership turmoil before Roux de Bezieux took over.
measurement.expected:
PROTESTS AND SOCIAL TENSION: Almost certain that the 100,000-plus Yellow Vest rallies and student protests will continue into next week, possibly with larger numbers as the minimum wage hike is digested and the public assesses whether it is enough. Probable that there will be at least one more day of clashes in Paris or major cities, given the momentum and the 'spiraling out of control' narrative. Possible that the government announces a second economic measure or a national dialogue to defuse the situation. Unlikely that the protests collapse entirely within a week.

IRAN FRIDGE HACK RETALIATION: Almost certain that France will announce a concrete response to the Iranian cyberattack, whether that is targeted sanctions, a cyber counter-operation, or a formal EU-level complaint. Probable that the diplomatic friction with Iran intensifies, with possible further ambassadorial exchanges or a temporary downgrade in relations. Possible that the US-China angle (Bessent tying it to a Chinese AI model) creates a minor trilateral discussion. Unlikely that France goes to full economic sanctions without broader EU backing.

EU SANCTIONS ON RUSSIA: Almost certain that the EU will approve the additional sanctions package on Russia on Monday November 16, as already announced. Probable that France pushes for specific measures targeting Russian energy or finance. Possible that the Russia-France tit-for-tat (lawmakers and journalists banned) produces a short diplomatic spat in the following days.

PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION MOMENTUM: Probable that at least one or two more candidates formally announce their 2027 candidacy in the coming days, as the Riner and Zemmour announcements have opened the floodgates. Possible that early polling shows a shift in the center or between the left-wing candidates (Mélenchon, Riner, Zemmour). Almost certain that the media will run extended profiles and debate coverage of the new entrants. Unlikely that any candidate drops out this week.

ECONOMY AND BONDS: Probable that French bond yields remain volatile and that the government faces pressure from ECB and markets to clarify its fiscal path. Possible that the government announces a mid-year budget revision or additional spending cuts in response to the Moody's downgrade. Almost certain that the minimum wage hike will be a talking point in both protest coverage and budget discussions. Possible that more corporate restructuring or office closures are announced, following Coty and IG Group.

FOOTBALL AND RUGBY: Almost certain that the French football team will regroup after the Italy defeat, with Zidane issuing post-match analysis and the squad preparing for the next Nations League fixture. Probable that Mbappé's return timeline becomes a major story. Possible that the rugby team's momentum from the South Africa win generates additional media attention and ticket demand for upcoming matches. Unlikely that another major injury crisis hits the football team this week.

AL FAYED PROBE AND JUSTICE: Probable that further searches, interviews, or arrests follow from the Ritz and Villa Windsor raids. Possible that new names are linked to the trafficking probe. Almost certain that the Depardieu case will generate continued media and social media debate. Possible that the Pissarro/Sotheby's annulment triggers further art-world legal disputes.

DIPLOMACY: Probable that the France-Algeria trade complaint at the EU level generates a short diplomatic exchange. Possible that the G7+ ports alliance sees its first operational steps. Almost certain that the France-Israel tension over Mélenchon's entry ban produces further commentary from both sides. Possible that the ECB succession discussion (de Cos vs. Lagarde) sees more media speculation.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES: A major new cyberattack on French infrastructure (energy grid, water, or transport) within the week. A second large-scale corporate bankruptcy or restructuring announcement. A sudden resignation or cabinet reshuffle triggered by the protest pressure. A surprise announcement that Lagarde will or will not run in 2027. A second shooting or attack targeting a specific community in Paris. A significant earthquake or natural disaster in the Fontainebleau or southern France region following the wildfire.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON: France calling a snap legislative election this week. A full-scale general strike halting all transport and industry. France formally breaking diplomatic relations with Iran or Israel. A no-confidence vote in the government. The ECB making a surprise rate decision specifically to help France. A major terrorist attack in Paris. France withdrawing from the EU or the euro. A second candidate dropping out of the 2027 race within seven days.

The Iran fridge cyberattack, the Al Fayed Ritz and Villa Windsor raids, the De Beers daylight robbery, and the Trappes suspect case all point to a week heavy on espionage, hacking, and police investigations.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the protest movement grew in both size and breadth. On November 9 the story was four consecutive weekends of demonstrations peaking at 575,000 to 600,000 people, led by students and unions. By November 14 the movement had widened into what Reuters and others called new Yellow Vest protests, with more than 100,000 rallying and the movement now explicitly touching workers, students, and the broader public. The escalation was fast: clashes in Paris on the 9th, Macron publicly condemning violence on the 10th, and students vowing to keep up pressure. The PM's minimum wage hike, which was a response in the first photo, became a test in the second. The Iran fridge cyberattack also grew, but in a diplomatic rather than a domestic direction. The first photo had France blaming Iran and vowing retaliation. The second photo shows France summoning Iran's ambassador, weighing sanctions, and the US Treasury Secretary Bessent adding a third-country angle by tying the attacks to a Chinese AI model. The 2027 presidential race expanded noticeably. Riner went from announcing a run to officially launching his candidacy and pushing back against being called a Macronist. Zemmour entered the race, a name not prominent in the first photo. Sarkozy issued a financial-crisis warning, and a poll showed Lagarde could rival the centrists. The rugby story resolved: France beat South Africa 21-19, a close win that confirmed the tight-match expectation. A new sports story appeared: France lost 3-1 to Italy in the Nations League, Zidane's first defeat, with Mbappé and Thuram both injured. The economy darkened. The first photo had Fitch downgrading the outlook and the budget rejected by parliament. The second photo shows Moody's cutting 2026 growth to 0.2 percent, French bonds under pressure, the ECB's Lane saying the problem must be fixed in Paris, and companies like Coty and IG Group cutting French operations. Diplomacy broadened: the G7 met as expected, but new threads appeared including France criticizing Israel over the Mélenchon entry ban, France and Germany backing Spain's de Cos for the ECB, a G7+ ports alliance, and a French-speaking nations summit in Cambodia. Several themes from the first photo vanished or shrank: the avian flu risk, the bus crash, the doping ban, the Paris Masters tennis results, and the specific Fitch downgrade all faded. New themes appeared that had no counterpart in the first photo: the Al Fayed probe with police searching the Ritz and Villa Windsor, a De Beers robbery, the Fontainebleau wildfire, the Macrons suing Joe Rogan, Russia banning French lawmakers and journalists, and 2030 Winter Olympics leadership turmoil. The overall tempo of the week was faster and more fragmented than the first photo suggested, with multiple crises running in parallel rather than one dominant story.
delta.wind: On protests, the expectation was almost certain for a fifth weekend, and that is exactly what happened with more than 100,000 people rallying. The expectation of further clashes in Paris, Lyon, and Marseille came true, with the Paris clashes on November 9. The Yellow Vests pushing mass disobedience came true in form, as the November 14 rally was explicitly described as new Yellow Vest protests. The PM's minimum wage hike being tested in the streets also came true. On the G7, the expectation that Rubio would be in Paris and the Iran cyberattack would be central came true. The expectation of a coordinated response or sanctions weighing came true as France summoned the ambassador and weighed sanctions. The expectation of a framework for European involvement in Ukraine talks was partially met, with the US seeking Europe's greater say. On rugby, the expectation of a tight, high-stakes match came true in the strongest sense: 21-19, a one-point margin, with Dupont at fly-half after only one training session. The expectation that it would not be a blowout was correct. The expectation that France might win came true. On the cyberattack fallout, the expectation that France would announce or hint at retaliatory measures came true with the ambassador summons and sanctions weighing. The expectation of no full diplomatic rupture was correct, with Iran denying involvement. However, the Credit Mutuel Arkea heist and a parliamentary inquiry, both listed as possible, did not surface prominently in the second photo, which is a miss. On the 2027 race, the expectation of Riner generating media attention came true, with his official announcement and the poisoned kiss exchange. The expectation of Mélenchon and Le Pen sparring came true, with Mélenchon eyeing a runoff against Le Pen. The expectation of no formal primary was correct. However, Zemmour entering the race was listed under things I would not bet on, and it happened, along with Sarkozy's financial warning and the Lagarde poll, which were not anticipated. On the economy, the expectation that the budget impasse would continue came true. The expectation that the Fitch downgrade would keep debt costs in the headlines came true but in a different form: Moody's replaced Fitch as the rating agency in the headlines, cutting growth to 0.2 percent. The expectation that the Bank of France would cut its GDP forecast came true in substance, with the central bank saying France would dodge a year-end recession but by a thin margin. The expectation of no full fiscal crisis or no-confidence vote was correct. On defense, the expectation of operational details on the NATO hub or MBDA order did not surface prominently, which is a partial miss. The expectation of no major new defense announcement was mostly correct, though the French army AI center was a small addition. The biggest surprise was the Al Fayed probe developments, the Fontainebleau wildfire, the Macrons versus Rogan lawsuit, and Russia banning French lawmakers, none of which were in the expectation. The things I would not bet on mostly held: no government collapse, no state of emergency, no new PM, no referendum, no coup, and the rugby match was not cancelled. The one thing from the do-not-bet list that partially happened was a new presidential candidate entering, with Zemmour. Overall, the expectations were broadly well-calibrated on the big themes of protests, rugby, G7, and the cyberattack, but underweighted the 2027 race's expansion, the economic deterioration's speed, and the miscellaneous legal and cultural stories that accumulate in a busy French week.
delta.driver: The force pushing France from the first photograph to the second is a compounding of domestic fiscal strain and social frustration that the government is trying to manage with half-measures while simultaneously projecting external strength. The cost-of-living squeeze, education funding gaps, and wage stagnation that started the student protests have now merged with the Yellow Vests' broader anti-government energy, creating a multi-actor opposition that is harder to negotiate with than a single union or student body. The government's minimum wage hike and social conference are visible attempts to buy time, but the Moody's cut to 0.2 percent growth and the bond-market pressure make every fiscal concession more expensive and more politically risky. Into this domestic pressure cooker, the Iran fridge cyberattack landed as an external shock that forced France to summon an ambassador, weigh sanctions, and coordinate with the G7, all while the streets were still hot. The 2027 race intensifies because every candidate sees the instability as both a threat and an opportunity: Riner and Zemmour offer a break from the existing parties, Mélenchon and Le Pen point to the government's inability to deliver, and even Lagarde is now being polled as a centrist alternative. The result is a country that is simultaneously protesting, negotiating, fighting a cyber war, restructuring its economy, and auditioning for a presidential race, all in the same five-day window, and the speed at which these threads tangle is what makes the second photograph feel more crowded and more urgent than the first.

crystal.eli5:
France is having a really rough stretch. For five weekends in a row, hundreds of thousands of people have been marching in the streets, and this week it got even bigger because now it is not just students, but also workers and the so-called Yellow Vests, a group that has been protesting about the cost of living for years. The government tried to calm everyone down by raising the minimum wage sooner than planned, but the mood is still angry. Next week, around November 21, we should expect another big protest, probably with more people than last week, and maybe some clashes in the cities. The government will probably try to announce a big meeting about social issues or add another small economic perk to keep the peace, but it is hard to satisfy a crowd that is made up of so many different groups with so many different demands.

At the same time, France is in a weird fight with Iran over a cyberattack that messed with supermarket refrigerators across Europe. France has already called in the Iranian ambassador, which is a strong diplomatic move, and next week we should expect France to announce something concrete, like sanctions or a formal complaint at the United Nations. The United States got involved too, saying the attack might have used a Chinese AI tool, which makes the whole thing a three-way headache for French diplomats.

The economy is not helping. A big rating agency just said France will barely grow at all this year, and companies are cutting jobs and closing offices. The government is trying to point to good things, like a new green hydrogen plant and money for farmers, but the overall feeling in the financial press is that France is walking toward a wall.
